title: The question I wish I had asked before trusting an automated system: does the stop button work when it's already broken?
author: henryzhangpku
selftext:
Every automated trading product ships the same safety list. Max risk per trade. Daily loss stop. Kill switch. After building one, I think that list is nearly useless for telling these products apart, because the list describes the happy path.

The question that separates them: does the stop control work when the system is already broken?

Not when everything is fine. Anyone's stop button works then. When the broker authorization has expired mid-session, when the runner has errored, when a position is open and the state is wrong — that is when a human reaches for the stop. That is the only moment the control exists for.

We shipped a version where it did not work in that moment, and I want to describe the shape of it, because it is a category of bug rather than a one-off.

Our session controls rendered when a session was "running." Reasonable. But a session can be alive without being healthy: broker auth expires, the runner errors, risk halts it. In those states the session is not "running" in the tidy sense, and our controls, written from the happy path, took that literally. Stop was rendered for the healthy states and withheld from the broken ones.

So the control that existed for emergencies was present in every situation except an emergency. One paper session sat unstoppable for 218 hours while the interface advised stopping it. And because a live session holds its broker account, the account could not be disconnected either.

We found three more instances of the same shape in the same week. A reset control that rendered correctly but sat inside a scrollable panel, so the mouse wheel scrolled the page instead and it could never be reached. A disconnect that refused when there was nothing to disconnect, aborting before cleanup, so the dead entry became permanent. And a removal that reported success while the underlying record survived, so it appeared to work and changed nothing.

One sentence for all four: the escape hatch was missing from the exact state it was built for.

This happens because guards get written from the author's mental model, and the author is imagining the feature working. "Show stop while running." "Throw if not connected." Broken states are, by definition, the ones nobody pictured. In most software that costs you an afternoon. In trading it holds a position.

If you are evaluating anything that touches a brokerage account — including your own code — these are the questions I would ask now:

1. Can I stop it when it is broken, not when it is healthy? Ask specifically what happens to the stop control when broker auth expires mid-session.
2. If a session is wedged and holding the account, can I still disconnect the broker, or does the wedge hold it hostage?
3. Does "removed" mean removed? Disconnect something, then check from a different device. If it comes back, it was never gone.
4. On a failed price read, does it size the position from stale data, or refuse? A system that treats a failed read as a valid answer will size against a number that does not exist.
5. Can you see what it did afterwards? Not a P&L number — the decisions, timestamped and reviewable.

Questions 1 to 3 are cheap to claim and expensive to build, which is exactly why they are the ones most likely to be untrue.

Where we landed: terminal states hide a recovery control, every other state keeps it. A refusal never aborts before cleanup, because the thing it refuses then becomes permanent. And a destructive-action lock asks "could this actually cause harm right now?" rather than "is something technically still open?"

Disclosure: I build a trading agent commercially, so I am not a neutral party here. I have deliberately not named it or linked it. The five questions are the useful part, and they apply to anything you run, including code you wrote yourself.

comments.author: Interesting_Gold_792
comments.body:
This is one of the most important distinctions I’ve seen made about trading-system safety.

I’m building and paper-testing an automated system, and this made me realize that having a kill switch is not enough if it depends on the same session state, UI, or runner that may already be broken.

The part about verifying the underlying state instead of trusting a successful UI response is especially important.

When you redesigned the recovery path, did you make it independently query the broker as the source of truth, or does it still rely on parts of the main session infrastructure?

I’m also curious whether you now test this through deliberate failure injection, such as expired authorization, stale prices, mismatched positions, or a frozen runner.
